# MPM Creature Breach

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y16j3XTaX-Q)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video demonstrates a multi-resolution MPM pipeline for a creature (the "Brute" character included with H21) breaching through terrain. The setup uses a low-resolution MPM simulation to identify fracture zones, then concentrates a high-resolution simulation only where detail is needed -- reducing particle counts from an estimated 1 billion (full volume) to roughly 88 million renderable points. The workflow also covers animated deforming colliders, velocity-clamped character animation, dynamic-to-static terrain masking, orient-based retargeting onto ultra-high-resolution point clouds, and secondary debris emission driven by density-based wind resistance.

## Key Concepts

### Terrain and Asset Preparation

The terrain starts from a grid with procedural noise applied for natural ground variation. A mountain asset is capped and placed at the breach point. Rock assets are scattered across the terrain for additional environmental detail. The camera is positioned to capture the creature emerging from the mountain.

### Character Animation with Velocity Clamping

The animated character ("Brute," packaged with H21) is imported as an Alembic. A high-resolution version with proper UVs is retargeted onto the low-resolution animation using Point Deform. Critically, an "enforce max velocity" wrangle limits per-frame displacement to a maximum of 0.25 units. The wrangle computes the delta between the current and previous frame positions, and if displacement exceeds 0.25, it clamps to that maximum multiplied by the displacement direction. This prevents MPM material from exploding when the animation moves too fast (especially at the feet and toes).

### Motion Trail Masking for Dynamic/Static Split

A motion trail is built by sampling the character's position across multiple frames throughout the frame range (the same technique used in the wolf snow scene). This trail is converted to an SDF mask and used as a stencil to carve the terrain into two regions: a dynamic patch that will be simulated with MPM, and the remaining terrain that becomes a static collider. This avoids simulating the entire terrain.

### Low-Resolution Simulation for Fracture Detection

The first MPM simulation runs at coarse resolution (particle separation 0.11) using the soil preset with stiffness multiplied by 160. Noise is applied to vary the stiffness spatially. Stickiness is enabled on both the animated character collider and the static ground to make soil adhere to the creature's arms. After the simulation completes, the maximum Jp (determinant of deformation gradient) attribute is gathered across all frames to create a fracture map. Regions that never fracture (Jp stays low, shown as blue) contain points that can be safely removed.

### Adaptive Resolution via Fracture-Guided Upsampling

The low-resolution simulation's Jp map is used to blast out all points in fracturing regions while keeping non-fracturing areas intact. The non-fracturing points are converted into a static collider. A second, higher-resolution MPM simulation (particle separation 0.06, nearly 8x the particle count in 3D) is then run only in the fracturing regions. The low-resolution collider guides the high-resolution simulation. Friction and stickiness on this collider are set extremely high to make high-resolution particles feel fully connected to the low-resolution pieces, hiding the resolution boundary.

### Ultra-High-Resolution Render Point Cloud

For the final renderable surface, even higher resolution points (particle separation 0.04) are scattered into the dynamic ground patch, yielding approximately 166 million points. A narrow-band pruning pass removes all interior points, keeping only those near the surface and crack regions, reducing the count to approximately 88 million. If the full volume were filled at this resolution, it would require roughly 1 billion points.

Each render point is assigned to its nearest MPM simulation point (from both low-res and high-res sims combined) using a proximity lookup with added noise to avoid perfect Voronoi cell boundaries. At each frame, the render points are placed at rest position, then the orient quaternion from the MPM solver is converted to a 3x3 matrix and applied to rotate them, and finally they are translated back into animated space. This retargets the MPM dynamics onto the ultra-high-resolution point cloud without re-simulating at that resolution.

### Secondary Debris

Both MPM simulations are combined into a single collider for the debris pass. Debris emission is driven by minimum Jp (stretching) and minimum speed thresholds, both animated over time: early frames emit more debris, and the thresholds ramp up later to prevent the particle count from growing unmanageable. Point density (neighbor count) drives wind and air resistance -- isolated particles catch more wind, while densely packed clusters resist it. Collisions are handled within the secondary POP simulation.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source | Convert terrain patch to MPM particles | Preset: soil; stiffness multiplied by 160 |
| MPM Solver | Run low-res and high-res simulations | Default settings; stickiness enabled on colliders |
| MPM Collider (static ground) | Static terrain collision | Stickiness enabled |
| MPM Collider (character) | Animated deforming collider for Brute | Animated deforming mode; stickiness enabled |
| MPM Collider (low-res sim) | Guide high-res sim with low-res results | Friction and stickiness set very high |
| MPM Source (high-res) | Source for second simulation pass | Particle separation: 0.06 |
| MPM Surface | Post-process for collider representation | Dilation: 1, smooth: 1, erosion: 4 |
| MPM Debris Source | Emit secondary debris particles | Min Jp and min speed animated over time |
| Attribute Wrangle (velocity clamp) | Enforce max displacement per frame | Max displacement: 0.25 units |
| Point Deform | Transfer animation to high-res character mesh | Standard usage |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Build the terrain** -- Create a grid, apply noise, place a mountain asset at the breach point, and scatter rock assets across the surface.
2. **Prepare the character animation** -- Import the Brute Alembic, enforce a maximum per-frame displacement of 0.25 using a wrangle, and Point Deform the high-res UV'd mesh onto the low-res animation.
3. **Generate the dynamic/static mask** -- Sample the character position across all frames to build a motion trail SDF, then carve the terrain into dynamic (MPM-simulated) and static (collider) regions.
4. **Run the low-resolution MPM simulation** -- Source the dynamic terrain patch at particle separation 0.11 with the soil preset (stiffness x160, noise-varied). Use the character as an animated deforming collider with stickiness.
5. **Analyze fracture zones** -- Gather the maximum Jp attribute across all frames. Blast fracturing points and convert non-fracturing regions into a static collider.
6. **Run the high-resolution MPM simulation** -- Source only the fracturing region at particle separation 0.06. Use the low-resolution non-fracturing points as a high-friction, high-stickiness collider to guide the simulation.
7. **Build the ultra-high-resolution render cloud** -- Fill the dynamic ground patch at particle separation 0.04 (~166M points). Prune to a narrow band (~88M points). Assign each render point to its nearest MPM point with noise-jittered proximity.
8. **Retarget dynamics onto the render cloud** -- At each frame, place render points at rest, apply the orient quaternion from the MPM solver as a 3x3 rotation matrix, then translate back to animated space. Compute velocity for motion blur.
9. **Simulate secondary debris** -- Combine both MPM sims as colliders. Emit debris particles driven by animated Jp and speed thresholds. Drive wind/air resistance by neighbor density. Handle collisions in a POP solver.
10. **Cache and render** -- Set the pscale attribute, store the rest attribute for shading, and cache all layers for rendering.

## Tips & Insights

- Enforcing a maximum displacement of 0.25 per frame on the character animation prevents MPM material from blowing up due to fast-moving extremities (feet, toes). This is a simple wrangle but solves a common problem with animated deforming colliders.
- The two-pass simulation strategy (low-res for fracture detection, high-res only where needed) is critical for production-scale scenes. Filling the entire volume at the final resolution would require approximately 1 billion particles, which would not fit on a standard GPU.
- Adding noise to the nearest-point assignment when retargeting onto the render cloud prevents visible Voronoi cell boundaries, creating more natural-looking fracture patterns.
- The narrow-band pruning of the ultra-high-resolution point cloud (keeping only surface and crack-facing points) reduces particle count by roughly half while preserving all visible detail.
- Animated deforming colliders are much more reliable in H21, making this multi-system pipeline practical for production.
- For secondary debris, animate the emission thresholds (minimum Jp and minimum speed) over time to front-load debris emission and prevent particle counts from becoming unmanageable in later frames.
- Density-based wind resistance (more neighbors = less wind effect) is a reusable pattern applied across all MPM masterclass scenes for natural-looking secondary particle behavior.

# MPM Train Wreck

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fwAuygMxk2w)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video walks through a large-scale metal destruction setup where a train derails, tumbles across terrain, and tears apart to reveal interior details. The pipeline covers surface-type MPM sourcing for thin-shell metal geometry, spatially varying friction via the new friction VDB feature, synthetic ground colliders for grip and tearing, consistent point count management for MPM post-processing, the "close gap" feature for realistic metal tears, and debris instancing with procedural rolling orientation. This is one of the most production-relevant examples in the masterclass, demonstrating how MPM handles continuous metal deformation and tearing that would be extremely difficult with traditional RBD approaches.

## Key Concepts

### Asset Preparation and Interior Detail

Two separate train models are combined: one provides the exterior shell and the other supplies interior details (seats, fixtures). The interior geometry is merged into the exterior model so that when the train tears open during simulation, the revealed interior reads as believable. Train track assets are similarly assembled from two source models to get the best combination of rail and ground detail.

### Surface-Type MPM Sourcing for Thin Geometry

Unlike the typical volume-fill approach, this setup uses the "surface" type on the MPM Source node to scatter particles only on mesh surfaces. This is appropriate for thin-shell metal geometry where a volume fill would either be wasteful or miss thin panels entirely. The "relax iterations" option is enabled to ensure even point distribution without holes. "Fuse overlapping points" is also enabled because the train has many panels near each other, and duplicate points at panel boundaries waste computation without adding detail.

### Metal Material with Compression Hardening

The metal preset is used as the base material. Compression hardening is increased from the default of zero to promote tearing over bending. With zero compression hardening, thin metal panels will bend and deform but resist breaking apart. Adding compression hardening makes the material more brittle, so it fractures and tears more readily. Stiffness is also increased so the train holds together as a rigid body until impact forces overcome the material strength.

### Spatially Varying Friction via Friction VDB

The H21 varying friction feature is used to create different friction zones on the collider. The rails are set to friction 0.5 (allowing the train to slide along them), while the ground and synthetic collider boxes are set to friction 1.25 (causing grip and tearing on contact). A friction attribute is defined per-point on the collider geometry, and the "friction create VDB from attribute" option generates a friction grid that the MPM solver samples during simulation. Ground plane friction is also increased separately on the solver.

### Synthetic Colliders for Grip and Tearing

Boxes and pointed collider shapes are placed along the ground where the train will tumble. These synthetic colliders serve two purposes: they prevent the train from sliding smoothly (which would look unrealistic) and they act as tearing agents that catch and rip the metal surface as the train rolls over them. Without these, the train would slide on the ground plane rather than gripping, rolling, and tearing open.

### Consistent Point Count for Post-Processing

The MPM container's bounding box deletes points that leave its domain. This creates a changing point count over time, which breaks the MPM Post Structure and MPM Deformed Pieces tools (they compare first-frame and per-frame point positions). The fix is a SOP-level pass that loops through all frames and freezes any deleted points at their last known position, ensuring constant point count. The frozen points are not rendered -- they exist solely to satisfy the post-processing requirement.

### MPM Fracture with Filler Points

The MPM Post Structure node generates fracture geometry from the simulation. Filler points are automatically added to ensure smooth deformation of non-fracturing regions (preventing linear, broken-polygon artifacts). The "align fracture to stretch points" toggle controls whether fracture centerlines align with the Jp stretch direction. For clean line tears, alignment works well. For large patch regions identified as fracturing, the un-aligned mode may produce better results. The presenter notes that the current scene may have excessive filler points and suggests reducing them if recreating the setup.

### Close Gap Feature for Metal Tearing

The "close gap" option on the MPM Deformed Pieces node fills small gaps and cracks that appear during metal tearing. Without it, fracture boundaries show unnatural sharp openings that do not read as torn metal. With it enabled, the gaps are filled with bridging geometry that creates a much more convincing metal-tear look. This is especially important for metal destruction where real-world tears produce bent, continuous surfaces rather than clean separations.

### Debris Instancing with Procedural Rolling Orientation

Secondary debris particles are split into two categories: sparks (rendered as points) and debris chunks (rendered as instanced geometry). For debris chunks, orientation is computed procedurally to simulate rolling. A rotation axis perpendicular to the velocity is calculated via cross product with an up vector. The angular velocity is derived from the particle's perimeter (2 * pi * radius, where radius is half of pscale), divided by the distance traveled per frame, multiplied by 2*pi to convert to radians. This is then scaled by 0.25 to reduce overly fast spinning on airborne debris. The angular velocity is stored in a custom attribute (not the standard `w`) to prevent the POP solver from overriding it, then remapped to `w` after the simulation for rendering.

### Debris Emission Pruning

Debris emission is manually controlled per frame range. Points existing before frame 47 are deleted entirely (no debris before the train starts breaking). At frame 58, 75% of existing debris points are randomly removed to reduce density. Emission is also ramped down from full to zero between frames 160 and 90 (later frames produce less debris). These are manual artistic adjustments to control the look and performance.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source (train) | Scatter particles on train surfaces | Preset: metal; type: surface; compression hardening: increased; stiffness: increased; relax iterations: on; fuse overlapping points: on |
| MPM Source (track/ground) | Collider geometry for terrain | Friction attribute: 0.5 (rails), 1.25 (ground/boxes) |
| MPM Solver | Run the train destruction simulation | Ground plane friction: increased; all else default |
| MPM Collider | Terrain and synthetic box colliders | Friction create VDB from attribute: enabled |
| MPM Surface | Build collider representation for secondaries | Default settings |
| MPM Debris Source | Emit secondary debris particles | Minimum stretching: reduced (more emission) |
| MPM Post Structure | Generate fracture geometry from sim | Filler points: present (possibly excessive); align fracture to stretch points: toggle |
| MPM Deformed Pieces | Retarget dynamics onto fractured geometry | Close gap: enabled; velocity computation: default |
| POP Solver (secondaries) | Simulate debris particles | Custom angular velocity via `www` attribute |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Prepare the train model** -- Combine exterior and interior train models so that torn-open panels reveal interior details (seats, fixtures).
2. **Build the track and synthetic colliders** -- Merge track models, add box and pointed colliders along the tumble path to provide grip and tearing surfaces.
3. **Source the train as MPM particles** -- Use surface-type scattering with the metal preset. Increase compression hardening for tearing. Enable relax iterations and fuse overlapping points.
4. **Set up spatially varying friction** -- Assign a friction attribute to collider geometry (0.5 on rails, 1.25 on ground). Enable friction VDB generation on the collider node.
5. **Run the MPM simulation** -- Increase ground plane friction on the solver. All other settings remain at default. The train derails, tumbles, and tears open.
6. **Fix point count consistency** -- Loop through all frames and freeze deleted points at their last position to ensure constant point count for post-processing tools.
7. **Generate fracture geometry** -- Use MPM Post Structure with filler points. Evaluate align-to-stretch mode versus default for the desired tear pattern. Reduce filler point count if excessive.
8. **Retarget with close gap** -- Use MPM Deformed Pieces to map simulation dynamics onto the fractured geometry. Enable close gap to fill unnatural cracks in the metal tears.
9. **Prepare debris for instancing** -- Extract small train fragments and rock assets, pack them as instanced geometry. Assign debris indices for Solaris instancing.
10. **Simulate secondary debris** -- Emit debris particles from the MPM sim. Compute rolling orientation via velocity-perpendicular axis rotation. Prune debris by frame range. Split into sparks and chunks.
11. **Set up Solaris rendering** -- Bring fractured train, debris instances, and secondary particles into Solaris. Assign debris indices to packed geometry for point instancing.

## Tips & Insights

- For thin-shell metal geometry, use surface-type sourcing rather than volume fill on the MPM Source node. Volume fill is wasteful for geometry that is essentially a shell.
- Compression hardening is the key parameter for controlling the balance between bending and tearing. Zero gives you flexible metal that bends; higher values produce brittle metal that fractures.
- The spatially varying friction VDB is essential for this type of setup. Low friction on rails lets the train slide into position; high friction on ground surfaces creates the grip needed for realistic tumbling and tearing.
- Synthetic colliders (boxes, pointed shapes) placed along the ground are a simple but effective way to force the train to catch and tear rather than slide. Real terrain is never perfectly smooth.
- Always ensure consistent point count before using MPM Post Structure and MPM Deformed Pieces. Freeze deleted points at their last position if the container prunes them.
- The close gap feature on MPM Deformed Pieces is critical for metal destruction. Without it, tears show unnatural clean separations rather than the bent, continuous surfaces expected of real metal.
- For debris rolling orientation, store angular velocity in a custom attribute (not `w`) during the POP solve to prevent the solver from overriding your procedural rotation, then rename to `w` after the sim.
- Scale the procedural rolling speed by 0.25 (or similar) to prevent overly fast spinning on airborne debris, which looks unnatural.
- Manual per-frame pruning of debris emission (deleting early particles, reducing density at specific frames) is a normal part of the artistic process for controlling the final look and performance.

# MPM Building Attack

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=beyRxMYzwsk)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This final practical scene in the MPM masterclass demonstrates building destruction driven by multiple projectile impacts. The pipeline covers converting non-watertight architectural models into fracture-ready volumes, adding internal structural support (pillars) to prevent unrealistic self-collapse, continuous emission of MPM projectiles with time-staggered impacts, the critical "assume unchanging material properties" optimization toggle, per-projectile fracture processing via for-loops with unique naming, consistent point count management for projectiles via reverse-time backtracking, and density-driven wind resistance for secondary debris. This is the most complex multi-system integration in the masterclass, combining the building as one MPM material with dynamically introduced projectiles of a different, stiffer material.

## Key Concepts

### Model Preparation for Destruction

Most architectural models from the internet (KitBash, SketchFab, etc.) are not usable for destruction simulation out of the box. They are modeled only for exterior visibility: surfaces are not closed, there are no convex hulls, and interior volume is undefined. The preparation process involves fusing vertices, closing holes to make the model watertight, and converting to VDB to establish a clear inside/outside boundary with uniform thickness. The result is a volumetric representation that can be fractured. UVs from the original model are transferred onto the prepared geometry afterward.

### Internal Structural Support

Internal pillars are added to the building geometry to support ceilings and floors. Without this internal structure, the MPM simulation will cause the building to collapse under its own weight immediately. This requires thinking like a civil engineer about how a real structure maintains its integrity. The pillars prevent self-collapse while still allowing destruction from projectile impacts.

### Building MPM Source Setup

The building is sourced using the concrete preset with stiffness doubled from the default. Noise is applied to the stiffness attribute spatially (the same noise-based variation pattern used in the creature breach scene) to create natural variation in material strength across the building surface. This prevents overly uniform fracture behavior.

### Projectile System Design

Projectile impact points are defined by scattering points on the target area of the building. Each projectile is assigned an impact frame distributed between frame 48 and frame 144 (3 x 48). The projectile positions are backtracked from their impact locations using their intended velocity and accounting for gravity, computing where each projectile needs to be at frame 1 to arrive at the building at the correct time. The trajectories appear to curve upward after impact in the viewport, but this is an artifact of the gravity extrapolation -- only the pre-impact portion of the animation matters.

### Projectile Emission via Domain Box

A bounding box ("domain box") is placed around the building. As each projectile point enters this box, it is grouped and its first-frame-of-entry is detected. On that specific frame, a sphere is copied onto the point, and MPM particles are emitted from it as a continuous source. This creates time-staggered emission: each projectile appears in the simulation at a different frame, matching its intended impact timing.

### Assume Unchanging Material Properties

The "assume unchanging material properties" checkbox on the MPM Solver is normally enabled as a performance optimization. In this scene, it must be disabled because the projectile material has significantly higher stiffness and density than the building material. When projectiles are introduced mid-simulation, the solver must reevaluate substep counts to accommodate the stiffer material. If the checkbox remains enabled, the solver will use substep counts calibrated only for the building material, causing the simulation to explode when the harder projectiles arrive. Disable this whenever continuously adding new materials with different properties during a simulation.

### Vibration Damping in Early Frames

Between the first frame and the frame where impacts begin (~frame 35), the building exhibits slight simulation vibration. This is addressed by freezing the simulation at frame 1 and frame 35, then linearly interpolating (lerping) between them. Alternatively, simply freeze-framing at frame 35 works equally well. This removes visual jitter in the pre-impact portion of the shot.

### Consistent Point Count for Projectiles

Projectiles are emitted at different frames, creating a changing point count that breaks the MPM post-processing tools. The solution reverses time: starting from frame 110 (when all projectiles have been emitted), the system solves backward to frame 1, gathering rest positions for all particles. For frames before a projectile's emission, its points are placed at a static rest position and backtracked linearly using the velocity at emission time. Two branches are maintained: one with the actual simulated animation, and one with the pre-emission static/extrapolated positions. As points appear in the simulation branch, they disappear from the static branch. When merged, the result is a smooth, constant-point-count animation suitable for post-processing.

### Per-Projectile Fracture via For-Loop

Each projectile is processed individually in a for-loop. The MPM Post Structure node generates fracture points for each projectile, and a namespace expression incorporating the loop iteration index ensures unique piece names across all projectiles (preventing name clashes during retargeting). Filler point separation is reduced to add more filler points, and the max distance parameter controls how far filler points extend from the MPM fracture region. Interior detail geometry is added to fracture pieces.

### Building Fracture Settings

For the building itself, the fuse distance is increased to prevent overly small fracture pieces. The minimum stretching threshold (minimum Jp) is increased to suppress fracture generation from low-deformation regions. The "align fracture to stretch points" toggle is presented as a matter of artistic taste for concrete: both aligned and un-aligned modes can produce convincing concrete fracture. The max distance parameter concentrates filler points near fracture regions, keeping memory and computation manageable for the large building model.

### Secondary Debris with Density-Driven Wind

Secondary debris follows the same pattern as the other masterclass scenes. Debris emission thresholds for both speed and stretching (Jp) are increased to limit particle count. The pscale is randomized for varied debris size. A debris index is assigned for instancing simple fractured-sphere geometry in Solaris. UV attributes are set per-debris-point to sample building textures for color variation. Point density (neighbor count) drives wind and air resistance: densely packed debris clusters (shown red) ignore wind, while isolated particles (shown purple) catch wind more aggressively. Debris rolling orientation uses the same velocity-perpendicular rotation setup from the train wreck scene.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| VDB From Polygons | Convert building model to watertight volume | Standard settings to establish inside/outside |
| MPM Source (building) | Generate MPM particles from building | Preset: concrete; stiffness: 2x default; noise on stiffness |
| MPM Source (projectiles) | Generate MPM particles from projectile spheres | Stiffness: very high; density: higher than building; continuous emission |
| MPM Solver | Simulate building destruction | Assume unchanging material properties: OFF |
| MPM Post Structure (projectiles) | Fracture each projectile via for-loop | Namespace with iteration index; reduced point separation; interior details |
| MPM Post Structure (building) | Fracture the building | Increased fuse distance; increased min Jp; max distance for filler concentration |
| MPM Deformed Pieces | Retarget dynamics onto fractured geometry | Default settings |
| MPM Surface | Build collider for secondaries | Default settings |
| MPM Debris Source | Emit secondary debris particles | Increased speed/stretch thresholds; reduced replication |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Prepare the building model** -- Fuse, close, and convert the architectural model to a watertight VDB with clear inside/outside. Add internal pillars for structural support. Transfer UVs from the original model.
2. **Source the building as MPM particles** -- Use the concrete preset with doubled stiffness and noise-varied stiffness across the surface.
3. **Design the projectile system** -- Scatter impact points on the building. Assign impact frames (48-144). Backtrack positions from impact using velocity and gravity to compute frame-1 positions.
4. **Set up projectile emission** -- Define a domain box around the building. Detect each projectile's first frame of entry. Copy spheres and emit MPM particles on that frame as continuous sources.
5. **Configure the solver** -- Disable "assume unchanging material properties" because projectiles have different (higher) stiffness and density than the building.
6. **Run the MPM simulation** -- Projectiles impact the building at staggered times, causing progressive destruction.
7. **Damp early-frame vibration** -- Lerp between frame 1 and frame 35 (or freeze-frame at 35) to remove pre-impact simulation jitter.
8. **Fix projectile point count** -- Reverse-solve from frame 110 to frame 1. Maintain two branches (simulated and static/extrapolated) and merge for constant point count.
9. **Fracture projectiles** -- Process each projectile in a for-loop through MPM Post Structure with unique namespace naming. Add filler points and interior detail.
10. **Fracture the building** -- Run MPM Post Structure with increased fuse distance, minimum Jp threshold, and concentrated filler points. Evaluate align-to-stretch mode for the desired concrete look.
11. **Retarget onto geometry** -- Use MPM Deformed Pieces to map simulation dynamics onto fractured building and projectile geometry with proper UVs.
12. **Simulate secondary debris** -- Emit particles from the MPM sim with controlled thresholds. Assign debris indices, randomize pscale, set UV attributes. Drive wind resistance by point density. Apply rolling orientation.
13. **Render in Solaris** -- Bring all layers (fractured building, projectile pieces, instanced debris) into the Solaris stage for final rendering.

## Tips & Insights

- Any internet-sourced architectural model will require cleanup for destruction work. Expect to fuse, close gaps, and convert to VDB before it is usable for MPM fracturing. The specific model does not matter -- the preparation process is the same.
- Internal structural support (pillars, cross-beams) is essential for building destruction. Without it, the building will collapse under gravity before any projectile arrives. Think about how real structures support themselves.
- Disable "assume unchanging material properties" whenever you introduce new MPM materials mid-simulation with different stiffness or density values. Leaving it enabled will cause the solver to use incorrect substep counts, leading to instability or explosion.
- The reverse-time backtracking technique for projectile point count consistency is reusable for any scenario with staggered MPM emission. Start from the frame where all particles exist, solve backward, and maintain a merged branch.
- For concrete fracture, the "align fracture to stretch points" toggle is a matter of artistic taste -- there is no single correct setting. Test both modes and choose the look that fits your shot.
- The max distance parameter on MPM Post Structure controls how far filler points extend from fracture regions. For large models, keeping this tight is critical for memory management.
- Assigning UV attributes to secondary debris particles and sampling the building's textures gives debris convincing color variation that matches the destroyed structure.
- The density-driven wind resistance pattern (dense clusters ignore wind, isolated particles catch it) is used consistently across all masterclass scenes and produces natural-looking secondary particle motion.
- Use unique fracture namespaces (incorporating for-loop iteration indices) when processing multiple objects through MPM Post Structure to prevent piece name collisions during retargeting.

# MPM Train Wreck

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fwAuygMxk2w)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video walks through a large-scale metal destruction setup where a train derails, tumbles across terrain, and tears apart to reveal interior details. The pipeline covers surface-type MPM sourcing for thin-shell metal geometry, spatially varying friction via the new friction VDB feature, synthetic ground colliders for grip and tearing, consistent point count management for MPM post-processing, the "close gap" feature for realistic metal tears, and debris instancing with procedural rolling orientation. This is one of the most production-relevant examples in the masterclass, demonstrating how MPM handles continuous metal deformation and tearing that would be extremely difficult with traditional RBD approaches.

## Key Concepts

### Asset Preparation and Interior Detail

Two separate train models are combined: one provides the exterior shell and the other supplies interior details (seats, fixtures). The interior geometry is merged into the exterior model so that when the train tears open during simulation, the revealed interior reads as believable. Train track assets are similarly assembled from two source models to get the best combination of rail and ground detail.

### Surface-Type MPM Sourcing for Thin Geometry

Unlike the typical volume-fill approach, this setup uses the "surface" type on the MPM Source node to scatter particles only on mesh surfaces. This is appropriate for thin-shell metal geometry where a volume fill would either be wasteful or miss thin panels entirely. The "relax iterations" option is enabled to ensure even point distribution without holes. "Fuse overlapping points" is also enabled because the train has many panels near each other, and duplicate points at panel boundaries waste computation without adding detail.

### Metal Material with Compression Hardening

The metal preset is used as the base material. Compression hardening is increased from the default of zero to promote tearing over bending. With zero compression hardening, thin metal panels will bend and deform but resist breaking apart. Adding compression hardening makes the material more brittle, so it fractures and tears more readily. Stiffness is also increased so the train holds together as a rigid body until impact forces overcome the material strength.

### Spatially Varying Friction via Friction VDB

The H21 varying friction feature is used to create different friction zones on the collider. The rails are set to friction 0.5 (allowing the train to slide along them), while the ground and synthetic collider boxes are set to friction 1.25 (causing grip and tearing on contact). A friction attribute is defined per-point on the collider geometry, and the "friction create VDB from attribute" option generates a friction grid that the MPM solver samples during simulation. Ground plane friction is also increased separately on the solver.

### Synthetic Colliders for Grip and Tearing

Boxes and pointed collider shapes are placed along the ground where the train will tumble. These synthetic colliders serve two purposes: they prevent the train from sliding smoothly (which would look unrealistic) and they act as tearing agents that catch and rip the metal surface as the train rolls over them. Without these, the train would slide on the ground plane rather than gripping, rolling, and tearing open.

### Consistent Point Count for Post-Processing

The MPM container's bounding box deletes points that leave its domain. This creates a changing point count over time, which breaks the MPM Post Structure and MPM Deformed Pieces tools (they compare first-frame and per-frame point positions). The fix is a SOP-level pass that loops through all frames and freezes any deleted points at their last known position, ensuring constant point count. The frozen points are not rendered -- they exist solely to satisfy the post-processing requirement.

### MPM Fracture with Filler Points

The MPM Post Structure node generates fracture geometry from the simulation. Filler points are automatically added to ensure smooth deformation of non-fracturing regions (preventing linear, broken-polygon artifacts). The "align fracture to stretch points" toggle controls whether fracture centerlines align with the Jp stretch direction. For clean line tears, alignment works well. For large patch regions identified as fracturing, the un-aligned mode may produce better results. The presenter notes that the current scene may have excessive filler points and suggests reducing them if recreating the setup.

### Close Gap Feature for Metal Tearing

The "close gap" option on the MPM Deformed Pieces node fills small gaps and cracks that appear during metal tearing. Without it, fracture boundaries show unnatural sharp openings that do not read as torn metal. With it enabled, the gaps are filled with bridging geometry that creates a much more convincing metal-tear look. This is especially important for metal destruction where real-world tears produce bent, continuous surfaces rather than clean separations.

### Debris Instancing with Procedural Rolling Orientation

Secondary debris particles are split into two categories: sparks (rendered as points) and debris chunks (rendered as instanced geometry). For debris chunks, orientation is computed procedurally to simulate rolling. A rotation axis perpendicular to the velocity is calculated via cross product with an up vector. The angular velocity is derived from the particle's perimeter (2 * pi * radius, where radius is half of pscale), divided by the distance traveled per frame, multiplied by 2*pi to convert to radians. This is then scaled by 0.25 to reduce overly fast spinning on airborne debris. The angular velocity is stored in a custom attribute (not the standard `w`) to prevent the POP solver from overriding it, then remapped to `w` after the simulation for rendering.

### Debris Emission Pruning

Debris emission is manually controlled per frame range. Points existing before frame 47 are deleted entirely (no debris before the train starts breaking). At frame 58, 75% of existing debris points are randomly removed to reduce density. Emission is also ramped down from full to zero between frames 160 and 90 (later frames produce less debris). These are manual artistic adjustments to control the look and performance.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source (train) | Scatter particles on train surfaces | Preset: metal; type: surface; compression hardening: increased; stiffness: increased; relax iterations: on; fuse overlapping points: on |
| MPM Source (track/ground) | Collider geometry for terrain | Friction attribute: 0.5 (rails), 1.25 (ground/boxes) |
| MPM Solver | Run the train destruction simulation | Ground plane friction: increased; all else default |
| MPM Collider | Terrain and synthetic box colliders | Friction create VDB from attribute: enabled |
| MPM Surface | Build collider representation for secondaries | Default settings |
| MPM Debris Source | Emit secondary debris particles | Minimum stretching: reduced (more emission) |
| MPM Post Structure | Generate fracture geometry from sim | Filler points: present (possibly excessive); align fracture to stretch points: toggle |
| MPM Deformed Pieces | Retarget dynamics onto fractured geometry | Close gap: enabled; velocity computation: default |
| POP Solver (secondaries) | Simulate debris particles | Custom angular velocity via `www` attribute |

1. **Prepare the train model** -- Combine exterior and interior train models so that torn-open panels reveal interior details (seats, fixtures).
2. **Build the track and synthetic colliders** -- Merge track models, add box and pointed colliders along the tumble path to provide grip and tearing surfaces.
3. **Source the train as MPM particles** -- Use surface-type scattering with the metal preset. Increase compression hardening for tearing. Enable relax iterations and fuse overlapping points.
4. **Set up spatially varying friction** -- Assign a friction attribute to collider geometry (0.5 on rails, 1.25 on ground). Enable friction VDB generation on the collider node.
5. **Run the MPM simulation** -- Increase ground plane friction on the solver. All other settings remain at default. The train derails, tumbles, and tears open.
6. **Fix point count consistency** -- Loop through all frames and freeze deleted points at their last position to ensure constant point count for post-processing tools.
7. **Generate fracture geometry** -- Use MPM Post Structure with filler points. Evaluate align-to-stretch mode versus default for the desired tear pattern. Reduce filler point count if excessive.
8. **Retarget with close gap** -- Use MPM Deformed Pieces to map simulation dynamics onto the fractured geometry. Enable close gap to fill unnatural cracks in the metal tears.
9. **Prepare debris for instancing** -- Extract small train fragments and rock assets, pack them as instanced geometry. Assign debris indices for Solaris instancing.

- For thin-shell metal geometry, use surface-type sourcing rather than volume fill on the MPM Source node. Volume fill is wasteful for geometry that is essentially a shell.
- Compression hardening is the key parameter for controlling the balance between bending and tearing. Zero gives you flexible metal that bends; higher values produce brittle metal that fractures.

# MPM Building Attack

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=beyRxMYzwsk)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This final practical scene in the MPM masterclass demonstrates building destruction driven by multiple projectile impacts. The pipeline covers converting non-watertight architectural models into fracture-ready volumes, adding internal structural support (pillars) to prevent unrealistic self-collapse, continuous emission of MPM projectiles with time-staggered impacts, the critical "assume unchanging material properties" optimization toggle, per-projectile fracture processing via for-loops with unique naming, consistent point count management for projectiles via reverse-time backtracking, and density-driven wind resistance for secondary debris. This is the most complex multi-system integration in the masterclass, combining the building as one MPM material with dynamically introduced projectiles of a different, stiffer material.

## Key Concepts

### Model Preparation for Destruction

Most architectural models from the internet (KitBash, SketchFab, etc.) are not usable for destruction simulation out of the box. They are modeled only for exterior visibility: surfaces are not closed, there are no convex hulls, and interior volume is undefined. The preparation process involves fusing vertices, closing holes to make the model watertight, and converting to VDB to establish a clear inside/outside boundary with uniform thickness. The result is a volumetric representation that can be fractured. UVs from the original model are transferred onto the prepared geometry afterward.

### Internal Structural Support

Internal pillars are added to the building geometry to support ceilings and floors. Without this internal structure, the MPM simulation will cause the building to collapse under its own weight immediately. This requires thinking like a civil engineer about how a real structure maintains its integrity. The pillars prevent self-collapse while still allowing destruction from projectile impacts.

### Building MPM Source Setup

The building is sourced using the concrete preset with stiffness doubled from the default. Noise is applied to the stiffness attribute spatially (the same noise-based variation pattern used in the creature breach scene) to create natural variation in material strength across the building surface. This prevents overly uniform fracture behavior.

### Projectile System Design

Projectile impact points are defined by scattering points on the target area of the building. Each projectile is assigned an impact frame distributed between frame 48 and frame 144 (3 x 48). The projectile positions are backtracked from their impact locations using their intended velocity and accounting for gravity, computing where each projectile needs to be at frame 1 to arrive at the building at the correct time. The trajectories appear to curve upward after impact in the viewport, but this is an artifact of the gravity extrapolation -- only the pre-impact portion of the animation matters.

### Projectile Emission via Domain Box

A bounding box ("domain box") is placed around the building. As each projectile point enters this box, it is grouped and its first-frame-of-entry is detected. On that specific frame, a sphere is copied onto the point, and MPM particles are emitted from it as a continuous source. This creates time-staggered emission: each projectile appears in the simulation at a different frame, matching its intended impact timing.

### Assume Unchanging Material Properties

The "assume unchanging material properties" checkbox on the MPM Solver is normally enabled as a performance optimization. In this scene, it must be disabled because the projectile material has significantly higher stiffness and density than the building material. When projectiles are introduced mid-simulation, the solver must reevaluate substep counts to accommodate the stiffer material. If the checkbox remains enabled, the solver will use substep counts calibrated only for the building material, causing the simulation to explode when the harder projectiles arrive. Disable this whenever continuously adding new materials with different properties during a simulation.

### Vibration Damping in Early Frames

Between the first frame and the frame where impacts begin (~frame 35), the building exhibits slight simulation vibration. This is addressed by freezing the simulation at frame 1 and frame 35, then linearly interpolating (lerping) between them. Alternatively, simply freeze-framing at frame 35 works equally well. This removes visual jitter in the pre-impact portion of the shot.

### Consistent Point Count for Projectiles

Projectiles are emitted at different frames, creating a changing point count that breaks the MPM post-processing tools. The solution reverses time: starting from frame 110 (when all projectiles have been emitted), the system solves backward to frame 1, gathering rest positions for all particles. For frames before a projectile's emission, its points are placed at a static rest position and backtracked linearly using the velocity at emission time. Two branches are maintained: one with the actual simulated animation, and one with the pre-emission static/extrapolated positions. As points appear in the simulation branch, they disappear from the static branch. When merged, the result is a smooth, constant-point-count animation suitable for post-processing.

### Per-Projectile Fracture via For-Loop

Each projectile is processed individually in a for-loop. The MPM Post Structure node generates fracture points for each projectile, and a namespace expression incorporating the loop iteration index ensures unique piece names across all projectiles (preventing name clashes during retargeting). Filler point separation is reduced to add more filler points, and the max distance parameter controls how far filler points extend from the MPM fracture region. Interior detail geometry is added to fracture pieces.

### Building Fracture Settings

For the building itself, the fuse distance is increased to prevent overly small fracture pieces. The minimum stretching threshold (minimum Jp) is increased to suppress fracture generation from low-deformation regions. The "align fracture to stretch points" toggle is presented as a matter of artistic taste for concrete: both aligned and un-aligned modes can produce convincing concrete fracture. The max distance parameter concentrates filler points near fracture regions, keeping memory and computation manageable for the large building model.

### Secondary Debris with Density-Driven Wind

Secondary debris follows the same pattern as the other masterclass scenes. Debris emission thresholds for both speed and stretching (Jp) are increased to limit particle count. The pscale is randomized for varied debris size. A debris index is assigned for instancing simple fractured-sphere geometry in Solaris. UV attributes are set per-debris-point to sample building textures for color variation. Point density (neighbor count) drives wind and air resistance: densely packed debris clusters (shown red) ignore wind, while isolated particles (shown purple) catch wind more aggressively. Debris rolling orientation uses the same velocity-perpendicular rotation setup from the train wreck scene.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| VDB From Polygons | Convert building model to watertight volume | Standard settings to establish inside/outside |
| MPM Source (building) | Generate MPM particles from building | Preset: concrete; stiffness: 2x default; noise on stiffness |
| MPM Source (projectiles) | Generate MPM particles from projectile spheres | Stiffness: very high; density: higher than building; continuous emission |
| MPM Solver | Simulate building destruction | Assume unchanging material properties: OFF |
| MPM Post Structure (projectiles) | Fracture each projectile via for-loop | Namespace with iteration index; reduced point separation; interior details |
| MPM Post Structure (building) | Fracture the building | Increased fuse distance; increased min Jp; max distance for filler concentration |
| MPM Deformed Pieces | Retarget dynamics onto fractured geometry | Default settings |
| MPM Surface | Build collider for secondaries | Default settings |
| MPM Debris Source | Emit secondary debris particles | Increased speed/stretch thresholds; reduced replication |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Prepare the building model** -- Fuse, close, and convert the architectural model to a watertight VDB with clear inside/outside. Add internal pillars for structural support. Transfer UVs from the original model.
2. **Source the building as MPM particles** -- Use the concrete preset with doubled stiffness and noise-varied stiffness across the surface.
3. **Design the projectile system** -- Scatter impact points on the building. Assign impact frames (48-144). Backtrack positions from impact using velocity and gravity to compute frame-1 positions.
4. **Set up projectile emission** -- Define a domain box around the building. Detect each projectile's first frame of entry. Copy spheres and emit MPM particles on that frame as continuous sources.
5. **Configure the solver** -- Disable "assume unchanging material properties" because projectiles have different (higher) stiffness and density than the building.
6. **Run the MPM simulation** -- Projectiles impact the building at staggered times, causing progressive destruction.
7. **Damp early-frame vibration** -- Lerp between frame 1 and frame 35 (or freeze-frame at 35) to remove pre-impact simulation jitter.
8. **Fix projectile point count** -- Reverse-solve from frame 110 to frame 1. Maintain two branches (simulated and static/extrapolated) and merge for constant point count.
9. **Fracture projectiles** -- Process each projectile in a for-loop through MPM Post Structure with unique namespace naming. Add filler points and interior detail.
10. **Fracture the building** -- Run MPM Post Structure with increased fuse distance, minimum Jp threshold, and concentrated filler points. Evaluate align-to-stretch mode for the desired concrete look.
11. **Retarget onto geometry** -- Use MPM Deformed Pieces to map simulation dynamics onto fractured building and projectile geometry with proper UVs.
12. **Simulate secondary debris** -- Emit particles from the MPM sim with controlled thresholds. Assign debris indices, randomize pscale, set UV attributes. Drive wind resistance by point density. Apply rolling orientation.
13. **Render in Solaris** -- Bring all layers (fractured building, projectile pieces, instanced debris) into the Solaris stage for final rendering.

## Tips & Insights

- Any internet-sourced architectural model will require cleanup for destruction work. Expect to fuse, close gaps, and convert to VDB before it is usable for MPM fracturing. The specific model does not matter -- the preparation process is the same.
- Internal structural support (pillars, cross-beams) is essential for building destruction. Without it, the building will collapse under gravity before any projectile arrives. Think about how real structures support themselves.
- Disable "assume unchanging material properties" whenever you introduce new MPM materials mid-simulation with different stiffness or density values. Leaving it enabled will cause the solver to use incorrect substep counts, leading to instability or explosion.
- The reverse-time backtracking technique for projectile point count consistency is reusable for any scenario with staggered MPM emission. Start from the frame where all particles exist, solve backward, and maintain a merged branch.
- For concrete fracture, the "align fracture to stretch points" toggle is a matter of artistic taste -- there is no single correct setting. Test both modes and choose the look that fits your shot.
- The max distance parameter on MPM Post Structure controls how far filler points extend from fracture regions. For large models, keeping this tight is critical for memory management.
- Assigning UV attributes to secondary debris particles and sampling the building's textures gives debris convincing color variation that matches the destroyed structure.
- The density-driven wind resistance pattern (dense clusters ignore wind, isolated particles catch it) is used consistently across all masterclass scenes and produces natural-looking secondary particle motion.
- Use unique fracture namespaces (incorporating for-loop iteration indices) when processing multiple objects through MPM Post Structure to prevent piece name collisions during retargeting.

# MPM Creature Breach

**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video demonstrates a multi-resolution MPM pipeline for a creature (the "Brute" character included with H21) breaching through terrain. The setup uses a low-resolution MPM simulation to identify fracture zones, then concentrates a high-resolution simulation only where detail is needed -- reducing particle counts from an estimated 1 billion (full volume) to roughly 88 million renderable points. The workflow also covers animated deforming colliders, velocity-clamped character animation, dynamic-to-static terrain masking, orient-based retargeting onto ultra-high-resolution point clouds, and secondary debris emission driven by density-based wind resistance.

## Key Concepts

### Terrain and Asset Preparation

The terrain starts from a grid with procedural noise applied for natural ground variation. A mountain asset is capped and placed at the breach point. Rock assets are scattered across the terrain for additional environmental detail. The camera is positioned to capture the creature emerging from the mountain.

### Character Animation with Velocity Clamping

The animated character ("Brute," packaged with H21) is imported as an Alembic. A high-resolution version with proper UVs is retargeted onto the low-resolution animation using Point Deform. Critically, an "enforce max velocity" wrangle limits per-frame displacement to a maximum of 0.25 units. The wrangle computes the delta between the current and previous frame positions, and if displacement exceeds 0.25, it clamps to that maximum multiplied by the displacement direction. This prevents MPM material from exploding when the animation moves too fast (especially at the feet and toes).

### Motion Trail Masking for Dynamic/Static Split

A motion trail is built by sampling the character's position across multiple frames throughout the frame range (the same technique used in the wolf snow scene). This trail is converted to an SDF mask and used as a stencil to carve the terrain into two regions: a dynamic patch that will be simulated with MPM, and the remaining terrain that becomes a static collider. This avoids simulating the entire terrain.

### Low-Resolution Simulation for Fracture Detection

The first MPM simulation runs at coarse resolution (particle separation 0.11) using the soil preset with stiffness multiplied by 160. Noise is applied to vary the stiffness spatially. Stickiness is enabled on both the animated character collider and the static ground to make soil adhere to the creature's arms. After the simulation completes, the maximum Jp (determinant of deformation gradient) attribute is gathered across all frames to create a fracture map. Regions that never fracture (Jp stays low, shown as blue) contain points that can be safely removed.

### Adaptive Resolution via Fracture-Guided Upsampling

The low-resolution simulation's Jp map is used to blast out all points in fracturing regions while keeping non-fracturing areas intact. The non-fracturing points are converted into a static collider. A second, higher-resolution MPM simulation (particle separation 0.06, nearly 8x the particle count in 3D) is then run only in the fracturing regions. The low-resolution collider guides the high-resolution simulation. Friction and stickiness on this collider are set extremely high to make high-resolution particles feel fully connected to the low-resolution pieces, hiding the resolution boundary.

### Ultra-High-Resolution Render Point Cloud

For the final renderable surface, even higher resolution points (particle separation 0.04) are scattered into the dynamic ground patch, yielding approximately 166 million points. A narrow-band pruning pass removes all interior points, keeping only those near the surface and crack regions, reducing the count to approximately 88 million. If the full volume were filled at this resolution, it would require roughly 1 billion points.

Each render point is assigned to its nearest MPM simulation point (from both low-res and high-res sims combined) using a proximity lookup with added noise to avoid perfect Voronoi cell boundaries. At each frame, the render points are placed at rest position, then the orient quaternion from the MPM solver is converted to a 3x3 matrix and applied to rotate them, and finally they are translated back into animated space. This retargets the MPM dynamics onto the ultra-high-resolution point cloud without re-simulating at that resolution.

### Secondary Debris

Both MPM simulations are combined into a single collider for the debris pass. Debris emission is driven by minimum Jp (stretching) and minimum speed thresholds, both animated over time: early frames emit more debris, and the thresholds ramp up later to prevent the particle count from growing unmanageable. Point density (neighbor count) drives wind and air resistance -- isolated particles catch more wind, while densely packed clusters resist it. Collisions are handled within the secondary POP simulation.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source | Convert terrain patch to MPM particles | Preset: soil; stiffness multiplied by 160 |
| MPM Solver | Run low-res and high-res simulations | Default settings; stickiness enabled on colliders |
| MPM Collider (static ground) | Static terrain collision | Stickiness enabled |
| MPM Collider (character) | Animated deforming collider for Brute | Animated deforming mode; stickiness enabled |
| MPM Collider (low-res sim) | Guide high-res sim with low-res results | Friction and stickiness set very high |
| MPM Source (high-res) | Source for second simulation pass | Particle separation: 0.06 |
| MPM Surface | Post-process for collider representation | Dilation: 1, smooth: 1, erosion: 4 |
| MPM Debris Source | Emit secondary debris particles | Min Jp and min speed animated over time |
| Attribute Wrangle (velocity clamp) | Enforce max displacement per frame | Max displacement: 0.25 units |
| Point Deform | Transfer animation to high-res character mesh | Standard usage |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Build the terrain** -- Create a grid, apply noise, place a mountain asset at the breach point, and scatter rock assets across the surface.
2. **Prepare the character animation** -- Import the Brute Alembic, enforce a maximum per-frame displacement of 0.25 using a wrangle, and Point Deform the high-res UV'd mesh onto the low-res animation.
3. **Generate the dynamic/static mask** -- Sample the character position across all frames to build a motion trail SDF, then carve the terrain into dynamic (MPM-simulated) and static (collider) regions.
4. **Run the low-resolution MPM simulation** -- Source the dynamic terrain patch at particle separation 0.11 with the soil preset (stiffness x160, noise-varied). Use the character as an animated deforming collider with stickiness.
5. **Analyze fracture zones** -- Gather the maximum Jp attribute across all frames. Blast fracturing points and convert non-fracturing regions into a static collider.
6. **Run the high-resolution MPM simulation** -- Source only the fracturing region at particle separation 0.06. Use the low-resolution non-fracturing points as a high-friction, high-stickiness collider to guide the simulation.
7. **Build the ultra-high-resolution render cloud** -- Fill the dynamic ground patch at particle separation 0.04 (~166M points). Prune to a narrow band (~88M points). Assign each render point to its nearest MPM point with noise-jittered proximity.
8. **Retarget dynamics onto the render cloud** -- At each frame, place render points at rest, apply the orient quaternion from the MPM solver as a 3x3 rotation matrix, then translate back to animated space. Compute velocity for motion blur.
9. **Simulate secondary debris** -- Combine both MPM sims as colliders. Emit debris particles driven by animated Jp and speed thresholds. Drive wind/air resistance by neighbor density. Handle collisions in a POP solver.
10. **Cache and render** -- Set the pscale attribute, store the rest attribute for shading, and cache all layers for rendering.

## Tips & Insights

- Enforcing a maximum displacement of 0.25 per frame on the character animation prevents MPM material from blowing up due to fast-moving extremities (feet, toes). This is a simple wrangle but solves a common problem with animated deforming colliders.
- The two-pass simulation strategy (low-res for fracture detection, high-res only where needed) is critical for production-scale scenes. Filling the entire volume at the final resolution would require approximately 1 billion particles, which would not fit on a standard GPU.
- Adding noise to the nearest-point assignment when retargeting onto the render cloud prevents visible Voronoi cell boundaries, creating more natural-looking fracture patterns.
- The narrow-band pruning of the ultra-high-resolution point cloud (keeping only surface and crack-facing points) reduces particle count by roughly half while preserving all visible detail.
- Animated deforming colliders are much more reliable in H21, making this multi-system pipeline practical for production.
- For secondary debris, animate the emission thresholds (minimum Jp and minimum speed) over time to front-load debris emission and prevent particle counts from becoming unmanageable in later frames.
- Density-based wind resistance (more neighbors = less wind effect) is a reusable pattern applied across all MPM masterclass scenes for natural-looking secondary particle behavior.

# MPM Train Wreck

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fwAuygMxk2w)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video walks through a large-scale metal destruction setup where a train derails, tumbles across terrain, and tears apart to reveal interior details. The pipeline covers surface-type MPM sourcing for thin-shell metal geometry, spatially varying friction via the new friction VDB feature, synthetic ground colliders for grip and tearing, consistent point count management for MPM post-processing, the "close gap" feature for realistic metal tears, and debris instancing with procedural rolling orientation. This is one of the most production-relevant examples in the masterclass, demonstrating how MPM handles continuous metal deformation and tearing that would be extremely difficult with traditional RBD approaches.

## Key Concepts

### Asset Preparation and Interior Detail

Two separate train models are combined: one provides the exterior shell and the other supplies interior details (seats, fixtures). The interior geometry is merged into the exterior model so that when the train tears open during simulation, the revealed interior reads as believable. Train track assets are similarly assembled from two source models to get the best combination of rail and ground detail.

### Surface-Type MPM Sourcing for Thin Geometry

Unlike the typical volume-fill approach, this setup uses the "surface" type on the MPM Source node to scatter particles only on mesh surfaces. This is appropriate for thin-shell metal geometry where a volume fill would either be wasteful or miss thin panels entirely. The "relax iterations" option is enabled to ensure even point distribution without holes. "Fuse overlapping points" is also enabled because the train has many panels near each other, and duplicate points at panel boundaries waste computation without adding detail.

### Metal Material with Compression Hardening

The metal preset is used as the base material. Compression hardening is increased from the default of zero to promote tearing over bending. With zero compression hardening, thin metal panels will bend and deform but resist breaking apart. Adding compression hardening makes the material more brittle, so it fractures and tears more readily. Stiffness is also increased so the train holds together as a rigid body until impact forces overcome the material strength.

### Spatially Varying Friction via Friction VDB

The H21 varying friction feature is used to create different friction zones on the collider. The rails are set to friction 0.5 (allowing the train to slide along them), while the ground and synthetic collider boxes are set to friction 1.25 (causing grip and tearing on contact). A friction attribute is defined per-point on the collider geometry, and the "friction create VDB from attribute" option generates a friction grid that the MPM solver samples during simulation. Ground plane friction is also increased separately on the solver.

### Synthetic Colliders for Grip and Tearing

Boxes and pointed collider shapes are placed along the ground where the train will tumble. These synthetic colliders serve two purposes: they prevent the train from sliding smoothly (which would look unrealistic) and they act as tearing agents that catch and rip the metal surface as the train rolls over them. Without these, the train would slide on the ground plane rather than gripping, rolling, and tearing open.

### Consistent Point Count for Post-Processing

The MPM container's bounding box deletes points that leave its domain. This creates a changing point count over time, which breaks the MPM Post Structure and MPM Deformed Pieces tools (they compare first-frame and per-frame point positions). The fix is a SOP-level pass that loops through all frames and freezes any deleted points at their last known position, ensuring constant point count. The frozen points are not rendered -- they exist solely to satisfy the post-processing requirement.

### MPM Fracture with Filler Points

The MPM Post Structure node generates fracture geometry from the simulation. Filler points are automatically added to ensure smooth deformation of non-fracturing regions (preventing linear, broken-polygon artifacts). The "align fracture to stretch points" toggle controls whether fracture centerlines align with the Jp stretch direction. For clean line tears, alignment works well. For large patch regions identified as fracturing, the un-aligned mode may produce better results. The presenter notes that the current scene may have excessive filler points and suggests reducing them if recreating the setup.

### Close Gap Feature for Metal Tearing

The "close gap" option on the MPM Deformed Pieces node fills small gaps and cracks that appear during metal tearing. Without it, fracture boundaries show unnatural sharp openings that do not read as torn metal. With it enabled, the gaps are filled with bridging geometry that creates a much more convincing metal-tear look. This is especially important for metal destruction where real-world tears produce bent, continuous surfaces rather than clean separations.

### Debris Instancing with Procedural Rolling Orientation

Secondary debris particles are split into two categories: sparks (rendered as points) and debris chunks (rendered as instanced geometry). For debris chunks, orientation is computed procedurally to simulate rolling. A rotation axis perpendicular to the velocity is calculated via cross product with an up vector. The angular velocity is derived from the particle's perimeter (2 * pi * radius, where radius is half of pscale), divided by the distance traveled per frame, multiplied by 2*pi to convert to radians. This is then scaled by 0.25 to reduce overly fast spinning on airborne debris. The angular velocity is stored in a custom attribute (not the standard `w`) to prevent the POP solver from overriding it, then remapped to `w` after the simulation for rendering.

### Debris Emission Pruning

Debris emission is manually controlled per frame range. Points existing before frame 47 are deleted entirely (no debris before the train starts breaking). At frame 58, 75% of existing debris points are randomly removed to reduce density. Emission is also ramped down from full to zero between frames 160 and 90 (later frames produce less debris). These are manual artistic adjustments to control the look and performance.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Source (train) | Scatter particles on train surfaces | Preset: metal; type: surface; compression hardening: increased; stiffness: increased; relax iterations: on; fuse overlapping points: on |
| MPM Source (track/ground) | Collider geometry for terrain | Friction attribute: 0.5 (rails), 1.25 (ground/boxes) |
| MPM Solver | Run the train destruction simulation | Ground plane friction: increased; all else default |
| MPM Collider | Terrain and synthetic box colliders | Friction create VDB from attribute: enabled |
| MPM Surface | Build collider representation for secondaries | Default settings |
| MPM Debris Source | Emit secondary debris particles | Minimum stretching: reduced (more emission) |
| MPM Post Structure | Generate fracture geometry from sim | Filler points: present (possibly excessive); align fracture to stretch points: toggle |
| MPM Deformed Pieces | Retarget dynamics onto fractured geometry | Close gap: enabled; velocity computation: default |
| POP Solver (secondaries) | Simulate debris particles | Custom angular velocity via `www` attribute |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Prepare the train model** -- Combine exterior and interior train models so that torn-open panels reveal interior details (seats, fixtures).
2. **Build the track and synthetic colliders** -- Merge track models, add box and pointed colliders along the tumble path to provide grip and tearing surfaces.
3. **Source the train as MPM particles** -- Use surface-type scattering with the metal preset. Increase compression hardening for tearing. Enable relax iterations and fuse overlapping points.
4. **Set up spatially varying friction** -- Assign a friction attribute to collider geometry (0.5 on rails, 1.25 on ground). Enable friction VDB generation on the collider node.
5. **Run the MPM simulation** -- Increase ground plane friction on the solver. All other settings remain at default. The train derails, tumbles, and tears open.
6. **Fix point count consistency** -- Loop through all frames and freeze deleted points at their last position to ensure constant point count for post-processing tools.
7. **Generate fracture geometry** -- Use MPM Post Structure with filler points. Evaluate align-to-stretch mode versus default for the desired tear pattern. Reduce filler point count if excessive.
8. **Retarget with close gap** -- Use MPM Deformed Pieces to map simulation dynamics onto the fractured geometry. Enable close gap to fill unnatural cracks in the metal tears.
9. **Prepare debris for instancing** -- Extract small train fragments and rock assets, pack them as instanced geometry. Assign debris indices for Solaris instancing.
10. **Simulate secondary debris** -- Emit debris particles from the MPM sim. Compute rolling orientation via velocity-perpendicular axis rotation. Prune debris by frame range. Split into sparks and chunks.
11. **Set up Solaris rendering** -- Bring fractured train, debris instances, and secondary particles into Solaris. Assign debris indices to packed geometry for point instancing.

## Tips & Insights

- For thin-shell metal geometry, use surface-type sourcing rather than volume fill on the MPM Source node. Volume fill is wasteful for geometry that is essentially a shell.
- Compression hardening is the key parameter for controlling the balance between bending and tearing. Zero gives you flexible metal that bends; higher values produce brittle metal that fractures.
- The spatially varying friction VDB is essential for this type of setup. Low friction on rails lets the train slide into position; high friction on ground surfaces creates the grip needed for realistic tumbling and tearing.
- Synthetic colliders (boxes, pointed shapes) placed along the ground are a simple but effective way to force the train to catch and tear rather than slide. Real terrain is never perfectly smooth.
- Always ensure consistent point count before using MPM Post Structure and MPM Deformed Pieces. Freeze deleted points at their last position if the container prunes them.
- The close gap feature on MPM Deformed Pieces is critical for metal destruction. Without it, tears show unnatural clean separations rather than the bent, continuous surfaces expected of real metal.
- For debris rolling orientation, store angular velocity in a custom attribute (not `w`) during the POP solve to prevent the solver from overriding your procedural rotation, then rename to `w` after the sim.
- Scale the procedural rolling speed by 0.25 (or similar) to prevent overly fast spinning on airborne debris, which looks unnatural.
- Manual per-frame pruning of debris emission (deleting early particles, reducing density at specific frames) is a normal part of the artistic process for controlling the final look and performance.
